qs.q: A 4-year-old child develops edema and hematuria 2 weeks after a skin impetigo infection. Urinalysis shows red cell casts. Which immunological mechanism is primarily responsible for this glomerulonephritis?
o: Type II hypersensitivity targeting glomerular basement membrane
Autoantibody production directed against streptococcal M protein

qs.e: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction involving immune complex deposition in the glomeruli.

ai.title: Impetigo
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Impetigo is a common superficial bacterial skin infection, usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. It spreads easily in crowded, low‑resource settings and may lead to complications such as cellulitis or post‑streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

sections.p: Impetigo presents as vesicles or pustules that rupture, leaving characteristic honey‑coloured crusts. It is most frequent in children but can affect any age, especially where hygiene is poor.
b: Highly contagious; spreads by direct contact or fomites

sections.p: The main pathogens are Staphylococcus aureus (including community‑acquired MRSA) and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A streptococcus). Both produce enzymes that break down skin barriers.
b: S. aureus: produces exfoliative toxins (ETA, ETB) causing bullous impetigo
S. pyogenes: produces streptolysins and pyrogenic exotoxins

sections.p: Bacteria colonise the anterior nares and skin folds. Minor trauma, insect bites, or eczema provide entry points. In low‑resource hospitals, overcrowding and shared linens accelerate spread.
b: Contaminated towels, clothing, or medical equipment

sections.p: Impetigo is a superficial epidermal infection. Two clinical forms exist: non‑bullous (crusted) and bullous (fluid‑filled). Complications include cellulitis, lymphangitis, and post‑streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).
b: Non‑bullous: honey‑coloured crusts on erythematous base
Bullous: larger flaccid vesicles that rupture, often on face or perineum

sections.p: Diagnosis is clinical; laboratory confirmation is reserved for atypical cases or outbreaks.

t.b: Identifies Gram‑positive cocci in clusters or chains; guides choice between staph and strep
Confirms organism and antibiotic susceptibility; if unavailable, treat empirically based on local patterns

t.a: Rapid antigen detection for group A strep (optional)
t.b: Helps when PSGN risk is high; positive result supports streptococcal etiology

sections.p: First‑line therapy targets the most likely pathogen while considering local resistance. Topical mupirocin is used for limited disease; oral therapy is required for extensive or bullous disease.
b: Topical mupirocin 2% ointment q.i.d. for <5 lesions
Oral amoxicillin‑clavulanate for widespread disease or bullous form
If MRSA prevalence >20%, use clindamycin or trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole instead of beta‑lactams

t.b: Determines topical vs systemic therapy; >5 lesions or facial involvement → systemic
Avoid nephrotoxic agents; choose drugs with safe renal profile

sections.p: Focus on pattern of lesions, exposure history, and complications. Remember that impetigo can be a portal for PSGN weeks later.
b: Bullous lesions on face of neonates suggest S. aureus exfoliative toxin
Ask about recent sore throat or skin infection to gauge PSGN risk

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid spread with fever, swelling, or lymphangitis
Development of hematuria or edema suggesting PSGN

faq.q: Can impetigo be caused by viruses?
faq.a: No, it is strictly bacterial; viral exanthems may mimic it but lack honey‑coloured crusts.

faq.q: Why is mupirocin preferred for limited disease?
faq.a: It concentrates at the skin surface, covers both staph and strep, and avoids systemic side effects.

faq.q: When should I suspect post‑streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
faq.a: If a patient develops hematuria, facial edema, or hypertension 1–3 weeks after a streptococcal skin infection.

exam: A child presents with honey‑crusted lesions on the face and a recent history of scratching; what is your immediate management — identify lesion type, decide topical vs oral therapy, and explain choice.
A patient with extensive bullous impetigo is HIV‑positive; which antibiotic regimen is optimal and why — discuss need for systemic therapy and MRSA coverage.
During a ward round you see a patient with impetigo and new onset periorbital edema; what complication are you concerned about and what investigation would you order — link to PSGN and urinalysis.
In a low‑resource clinic, Gram stain is unavailable; how do you decide empiric therapy for impetigo — use local epidemiology and lesion severity.

A neonate develops flaccid vesicles on the scalp that rupture quickly; which organism and toxin are most likely and why does this matter for infection control — answer with S. aureus exfoliative toxin and isolation precautions.
A community outbreak of impetigo occurs in a school; what public‑health measures reduce spread — emphasize hand hygiene, wound care, and temporary exclusion of affected children.
A patient on long‑term steroids develops impetigo that does not respond to mupirocin; what next step and why — consider systemic antibiotics and possible MRSA.
Explain why penicillin alone may be insufficient in areas with high MRSA prevalence — discuss resistance mechanisms and alternative agents.
